mainTopic: שוחד and a judge's fairness: borrowing, love and hate, bribes of words, and judges who stepped aside over small favors.
overview: This amud is about שוחד and how careful a judge must be to stay fair. It opens by warning that even a צדיק גמור who takes a bribe will end up confused, and that a judge who needs nothing, like a king, builds the land, while one who depends on others ruins it. רבה בר רב שילא rules that a judge who borrows without lending back is פסול. The גמרא defends this ruling against the case of רבא, who borrowed only to honor the lenders. רבא explains that a bribe makes the judge feel the giver is like himself, and רב פפא adds that a judge should not judge someone he loves or hates. A ברייתא teaches that even a favor without money, a 'bribe of words', is forbidden. Stories follow about great judges who stepped aside over tiny favors, and two of them admit that even a refused gift bent their thinking. Finally רב ענן accepts a gift given as a מצוה, but still sends the man's case to רב נחמן. The story of what רב נחמן said continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Even a righteous person who takes a bribe loses his clear mind
steps.stepSummary: The teaching about שוחד ends with a strong warning: even a צדיק גמור who takes a bribe will not leave the world without טירוף דעת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even a completely righteous person who takes a bribe will not leave this world without becoming mentally confused.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a warning about bribery that it started earlier. It says that even a truly righteous person is hurt by taking שוחד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being a צדיק does not protect you from what a bribe does. The punishment fits the sin: a bribe twists a judge's thinking, so in the end his mind becomes confused.

keyTerms.meaning: Mental confusion; losing one's clear mind

phrases.english: Even a completely righteous person who takes a bribe —
does not leave the world
without becoming mentally confused.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the bribery teaching that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking שוחד harms even a צדיק גמור, ending in טירוף דעת.

steps.title: A judge should be like a king, not like a priest collecting gifts
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports רב נחמן בר כהן's reading of משלי 29:4. A judge who needs nothing, like a king, builds up the land. A judge who goes around depending on others, like a כהן collecting תרומות at the threshing floors, ruins it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: רב נחמן בר כהן explained the verse 'A king establishes the land with justice, but a man of gifts destroys it.' If a judge is like a king, who needs nothing from anyone, he establishes the land. If he is like a כהן who goes around the threshing floors for his gifts, he destroys it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching that explains a פסוק. It shows how a judge's independence decides whether he helps the world or harms it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק contrasts a 'king' with an 'איש תרומות' (a man of gifts). רב נחמן בר כהן reads these as two kinds of judges. A judge who needs nothing can judge fairly. A judge who keeps asking others for things, the way a כהן goes from barn to barn for תרומה, will lean toward the people he depends on.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained a verse to teach a lesson
Gifts of produce given to a כֹּהֵן
Threshing floors, where grain is processed and תְּרוּמָה is given out

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the idea behind the next ruling: a judge must not be dependent on others. That is why borrowing can disqualify him.

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
Rav Nachman bar Kohen explained,
What is the meaning of what is written:
"A king establishes the land with justice,
but a man of gifts destroys it" —
phrases.notes: He reads 'man of תרומות' as someone who goes around collecting gifts, like a כהן.

phrases.english: if a judge is like a king,
who does not need anything —
"he establishes the land."
But if he is like a priest
who goes around the threshing floors —
"he destroys it."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אֲמַר: דָּרֵשׁ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר כֹּהֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of judges and bribery with a פסוק about a judge's independence.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge who is independent builds society. A judge who depends on others harms it.

steps.title: A judge who borrows things is disqualified
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב שילא rules that a judge who borrows items from others is פסול to judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב שילא said: A judge who borrows things is disqualified from judging.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a practical ruling. A judge who keeps borrowing from people may not judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Borrowing makes the judge depend on the lenders, and he owes them favors. This is the 'כהן at the threshing floors' kind of judge from the previous step, now turned into a halacha.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Sheila said:
This judge who borrows items —
is disqualified from judging cases.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא: הַאי דַּיָּינָא דְּשָׁאֵיל שְׁאֵילְתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the idea of a dependent judge into a practical disqualification.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge who borrows from others is פסול to judge.

steps.title: The rule applies only if he never lends in return
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב שילא limits his rule. It applies only when the judge has nothing to lend others. If he also lends, there is no problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: We said this only when he has nothing to lend out. But if he has things to lend, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The same אמורא narrows his own ruling. Only a judge who borrows without ever lending back is disqualified.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If borrowing goes both ways, it is a normal exchange between neighbors, and the judge does not owe anyone. The problem is only one-way borrowing, which leaves him in other people's debt.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when — a phrase that limits a ruling
We have no problem with it

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new opinion. רבה בר רב שילא is narrowing the same ruling he just gave.

phrases.english: And we said this only
when he does not have things to lend out,
but if he has things to lend out —
we have no problem with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלֵית לֵיהּ לְאוֹשׁוֹלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling of step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a judge who borrows without lending back is disqualified.

steps.title: But רבא borrowed without lending back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ruling: רבא borrowed from the house of בר מריון even though they never borrowed from him, and he still judged.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבא borrowed things from the house of בר מריון, even though they did not borrow from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ruling by pointing to how רבא acted. He did exactly the one-way borrowing that the ruling forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא was a judge and borrowed in a one-way way. If the ruling were true, רבא should have been disqualified, so it looks like the ruling cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? — opens a challenge
But look! — brings a contradicting case

phrases.english: Is that so?
But Rava borrowed items
from the house of bar Maryon

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא שָׁיְילִי מִינֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: even though they did not borrow from him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling in steps 3-4 using how רבא actually acted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a judge who borrows without lending back is פסול.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא, a judge, borrowed one-way from בר מריון's household, which would seem to disqualify him.

steps.title: רבא borrowed to give them honor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבא's case was different. He borrowed from them to raise their standing, not because he needed the items.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he wanted to make them important.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains that רבא's borrowing had a different purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling worries about a judge who depends on others. רבא did not need anything from them. He borrowed only so that people would see this family as important. Since he was not dependent on them, the ruling stays in place.
steps.whatToRemember: A judge who borrows one-way is פסול because he becomes dependent. If the borrowing does not come from need, such as רבא's, which was done to honor the lenders, it does not disqualify him.

phrases.english: There, he wanted to make them important.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the purpose of the borrowing was different.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's one-way borrowing looked like the same dependency that disqualifies a judge.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא borrowed to honor the family, not out of need, so the disqualification does not apply.

steps.title: Why a bribe twists a judge's thinking
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the reason behind the ban on bribes. Once a judge takes something from one side, he starts to feel that person is like himself, and no one sees guilt in himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Why is a bribe forbidden? Once the judge takes a bribe from someone, his mind draws close to that person, and that person becomes like his own self. And a person does not see guilt in himself.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the reason why a judge may not take a bribe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger is not only that the judge will knowingly cheat. Taking the gift makes him feel the giver is part of himself. People naturally cannot see their own faults, so he will not be able to see the giver's guilt either.

keyTerms.meaning: Like his own self (literally, 'like his body')
Guilt, the losing side of a case

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the Torah forbids a bribe even to a judge who means to rule honestly. The harm happens inside the judge's mind, without him noticing.

phrases.english: Rava said:
What is the reason for the bribe prohibition?
Once he accepts a bribe from him,
his mind draws close to him
and he becomes like his own self,
and a person does not see guilt in himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a judge borrowing items (Steps 3-6) to the deeper reason why taking from a litigant damages judgment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bribe makes the judge feel the giver is like himself, and since no one sees his own guilt, he cannot judge that person fairly.

steps.title: The word שוחד means 'he is one'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the word שוחד as 'שהוא חד', meaning the judge becomes 'one' with the giver.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does the word 'שוחד' mean? 'שהוא חד', that he is one with the giver.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the Hebrew word for bribe itself hints at רבא's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By splitting שוחד into 'שהוא חד', the word becomes a description of what a bribe does. The judge and the giver become 'one', which is exactly רבא's point that the giver becomes 'like his own self'.

phrases.english: What is 'שוחד'?
That he is one.
phrases.notes: A play on the sounds: שוחד sounds like שהוא חד, meaning the judge becomes one with the giver.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's reason (Step 7) with a reading of the word itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word שוחד hints that the judge becomes 'one' with the person who bribed him.

steps.title: Do not judge someone you love or hate
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that a person should not judge a case for someone he loves or someone he hates, because love hides guilt and hate hides merit.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: A person should not judge a case for someone he loves, and not for someone he hates. Someone he loves, he will not see any guilt in. Someone he hates, he will not see any merit in.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא carries רבא's idea further: even without any gift, love or hate can bend a judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bribe works by building closeness, and love already is closeness, so it blinds the judge the same way. רב פפא adds the opposite case too: hate makes a judge blind to the good side of someone's claim.

keyTerms.meaning: Merit, the winning side of a case

steps.whyThisMatters: This takes the bribe idea beyond money and gifts. Personal feelings alone can disqualify a judge from a case.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
A person should not judge a case
for someone he loves,
nor for someone he hates.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרָחֵים לֵיהּ — לָא חָזֵי לֵיהּ חוֹבָה,
phrases.english: One he loves, he does not see guilt in him;

phrases.aramaic: דְּסָנֵי לֵיהּ — לָא חָזֵי לֵיהּ זְכוּתָא.
phrases.english: one he hates, he does not see merit in him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא לֵידוּן אִינִישׁ דִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רבא's logic about bias from bribes to bias from love and hate.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge should not judge someone he loves or hates, since love hides guilt and hate hides merit.

steps.title: Why a whole town may love a scholar
steps.stepSummary: אביי says that when a תלמיד חכם is loved by everyone in his town, it is often not because he is better, but because he never rebukes them about מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: This Torah scholar whom the people of the town love, it is not because he is especially great. Rather, it is because he does not rebuke them in matters of Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי adds a side teaching about love: being loved by everyone can be a warning sign, not a compliment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A scholar who speaks up about מצוות will upset some people. If no one is ever upset with him, it may mean he is staying quiet when he should not be. This connects to רב פפא's theme of how love and hate work between a leader and his people.

keyTerms.meaning: A Torah scholar (a young, sharp תלמיד חכם)

phrases.english: Abaye said:
This Torah scholar
whom the townspeople love,
it is not because he is especially good,
but because he does not rebuke them
in matters of Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן דִּמְרַחֲמִין לֵיהּ בְּנֵי מָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the theme of love from רב פפא (Step 9) and applies it to a scholar and his town.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A scholar loved by the whole town is often loved because he does not rebuke them in matters of Heaven.

steps.title: רבא learns that people's feelings do not follow his rulings
steps.stepSummary: רבא tells how he first thought all of מחוזא loved him, then thought winners loved him and losers hated him, and finally realized their feelings had nothing to do with his rulings.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: At first I used to think all the people of מחוזא love me. Once I became a judge, I thought some of them hate me and some love me. Once I saw that the one who loses today wins tomorrow, I said: if they love me, they all love me, and if they hate me, they all hate me.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא shares a personal lesson about how people feel toward a judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As a judge, רבא assumed losers would resent him and winners would like him. But the same people lost one day and won the next, so his rulings could not be the cause of how they felt. Whatever they feel toward him, love or hate, is shared by everyone and does not depend on his judgments.

keyTerms.meaning: מחוזא, the town where רבא lived and judged
Is found liable, loses the case

steps.whatToRemember: A judge should not worry that his rulings make people love or hate him. The same people win and lose at different times, so their feelings are not tied to his rulings.

phrases.english: Rava said: At first I would say:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי בְּנֵי מָחוֹזָא כּוּלְּהוּ רָחֲמוּ לִי.
phrases.english: these people of מחוזא all love me.
Once I became a judge, I said:

phrases.aramaic: מִינַּיְיהוּ סָנוּ לִי וּמִינַּיְיהוּ רָחֲמוּ לִי.
phrases.english: some of them hate me and some of them love me.
Once I saw that whoever is found liable today
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: wins tomorrow, I said:
if they love, they all love me;
if they hate, they all hate me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of love and hate toward community figures, now from a judge's own experience.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People's love or hate toward a judge does not depend on how he rules in their cases.

steps.title: Even a bribe of words is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that 'ושוחד לא תקח' forbids more than money bribes. Since the Torah did not say 'בצע', meaning money gain, even a bribe of words is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'And you shall take no bribe.' There is no need to say a money bribe is forbidden. Even a bribe of words is also forbidden, since the Torah did not write 'you shall take no profit.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new section begins: a ברייתא widens the ban on bribes to include favors done with words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from the Torah's choice of word. Had it said בצע (money gain), the ban would cover only money. By using the broader word שוחד, the Torah includes any favor that makes the judge feel close to one side, even a non-money one.

keyTerms.meaning: A bribe of words, a favor done through speech

steps.whyThisMatters: This fits רבא's reason from Step 7. If the problem is the closeness a bribe creates, then a favor without money can create it too.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: 'And you shall take no bribe.'
There is no need to say a money bribe,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ שׁוֹחַד דְּבָרִים נָמֵי אָסוּר,
phrases.english: but even a bribe of words is also forbidden,
since it does not say 'you shall take no profit.'
phrases.notes: Had the פסוק said בצע, which means money gain, only money would be forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: which kinds of favors count as a bribe.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ban on bribes includes a bribe of words, because the Torah used the word שוחד rather than בצע.

steps.title: What counts as a bribe of words?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what a bribe of words actually looks like in practice.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is an example of a bribe of words?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks for a real-life example of the 'bribe of words' the ברייתא just mentioned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave the rule but did not explain what it covers. The answer, which comes next, will show what kind of favor without money still counts as a bribe.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: What is a case of a bribe of words?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a concrete example of the rule just taught in Step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real-life example of a bribe of words.

steps.title: שמואל refuses to judge after a man helps him off a ferry
steps.stepSummary: A man gives שמואל a hand getting off a ferry. When שמואל learns the man has a case, he disqualifies himself from judging it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example: שמואל was crossing a river on a ferry. A man came and gave him a hand. שמואל asked him, 'What are you doing here?' The man said, 'I have a case.' שמואל said, 'I am disqualified from judging your case.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 13 with a story. A small physical favor, helping someone off a boat, counts as a 'bribe of words' that disqualifies a judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No money changed hands, only a helping hand. Still, שמואל felt that the favor made him lean toward this man. This shows that שוחד can be any favor, not just cash.

keyTerms.meaning: What are you doing here? What is your business?
I am disqualified from judging your case

steps.confusionAlert: The text does not say the man was trying to bribe שמואל, and שמואל did not accuse him of it. Even an innocent favor can make a judge lean one way, so the judge steps aside.

phrases.english: Like that story of Shmuel,
phrases.notes: This is the answer to the question in step 13: what does a bribe of words look like?

phrases.english: who was crossing on a ferry.
A certain man came
and gave him his hand.
He said to him: What are you doing here?
He said to him: I have a case.
He said to him: I am disqualified from judging your case.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הֲוָה עָבַר בְּמַבָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13 with a real-life example.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A bribe of words can be a small personal favor, like helping a judge off a ferry.

steps.title: אמימר refuses to judge after a man removes a feather from his head
steps.stepSummary: While אמימר was judging, a feather landed on his head and a man removed it. When the man said he had a case, אמימר disqualified himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר was sitting and judging a case. A feather flew onto his head. A man came and removed it. אמימר asked, 'What are you doing here?' He said, 'I have a case.' אמימר said, 'I am disqualified from judging your case.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second story, with an even smaller favor: just taking a feather off the judge's head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This favor is tinier than helping someone off a boat. The point grows stronger: even the smallest kindness creates a bond that could bias a judge.

keyTerms.meaning: He took it away / removed it

phrases.english: Ameimar was sitting
and judging a case.
A feather flew onto his head.
A certain man came and removed it.
He said to him: What are you doing here?
He said to him: I have a case.
He said to him: I am disqualified from judging your case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר הֲוָה יָתֵיב וְקָא דָאֵין דִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second example of the same idea, with an even smaller favor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even removing a feather from a judge's head is a favor that disqualifies him from the case.

steps.title: מר עוקבא refuses to judge after a man covers spit in front of him
steps.stepSummary: There was spit on the ground in front of מר עוקבא, and a man covered it. When the man said he had a case, מר עוקבא disqualified himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was spit lying in front of מר עוקבא. A man came and covered it. מר עוקבא asked, 'What are you doing here?' He said, 'I have a case.' מר עוקבא said, 'I am disqualified from judging your case.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third story with the same pattern. This time the favor was covering something unpleasant on the floor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the previous stories, this was a small favor that saved the judge a bit of bother. Three great judges all treated such favors as real שוחד.

phrases.aramaic: מָר עוּקְבָא הֲוָה שְׁדֵי רוּקָּא קַמֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: There was spit lying in front of Mar Ukva.
A certain man came and covered it.
He said to him: What are you doing here?
He said to him: I have a case.
He said to him: I am disqualified from judging your case.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר עוּקְבָא הֲוָה שְׁדֵי רוּקָּא קַמֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third example of a small favor that disqualifies a judge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Covering spit in front of a judge is a favor that disqualifies him from the man's case.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל refuses his sharecropper's early fruit basket
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי's sharecropper usually brought him fruit every Friday. One week he brought it on Thursday because he had a case. רבי ישמעאל refused the fruit and disqualified himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי had a sharecropper who used to bring him a basket of fruit every Friday. One day he brought it on Thursday. רבי ישמעאל asked, 'Why is it different today?' He said, 'I have a case, so I thought I would bring it to the master on my way.' רבי ישמעאל did not accept it and said, 'I am disqualified from judging your case.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a fourth story. Here the gift was something the judge was going to get anyway, yet he still refused it and disqualified himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fruit really belonged to רבי ישמעאל, since the sharecropper worked his field. The only 'favor' was bringing it a day early, to save himself a trip. Even that small convenience was enough for רבי ישמעאל to step aside.

keyTerms.meaning: A sharecropper who works someone's field for a share of the crops
On my way, since I am coming anyway

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei:
his sharecropper was used to
bringing him
every Friday a basket of fruit.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד אַיְיתִי לֵיהּ בְּחַמְשָׁה בְּשַׁבְּתָא.
phrases.english: One day he brought it to him on Thursday.
He said to him: What is different now?
He said to him: I have a case,
and I said, since I'm on my way anyway,
I will bring it to the master.
He did not accept it from him.
He said to him: I am disqualified from judging your case.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הֲוָה רְגִיל אֲרִיסֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth story, where the 'gift' was something the judge already owned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even bringing a judge his own fruit early, for the litigant's convenience, is enough to disqualify him.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל feels himself leaning toward the sharecropper
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל appointed two other scholars to judge the case. As he walked back and forth, he kept thinking of arguments the sharecropper could use to win.
steps.simpleTranslation: He seated two rabbis, and they judged the sharecropper's case. As רבי ישמעאל was walking back and forth, he said to himself: 'If he wants, he could argue this way, and if he wants, he could argue that way.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. Even though רבי ישמעאל took nothing and was not the judge, his mind kept looking for ways for the sharecropper to win. This sets up his conclusion in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the surprise of the story. The offer alone, which he refused, was enough to pull his thinking toward one side. It proves that the judges in the earlier stories were right to be careful.

phrases.english: He seated a pair of rabbis,
and they were judging him.
As he was going and coming, he said:
If he wants, he can argue this way,
and if he wants, he can argue that way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of רבי ישמעאל and shows the effect the refused gift had on him.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a refused gift made רבי ישמעאל's mind lean toward the giver.

steps.title: How much more are bribe-takers biased
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל curses those who take bribes. He reasons with a קל וחומר: if he leaned toward the man without taking anything, people who actually take bribes are surely biased.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'May the souls of those who take bribes be blown away! If I, who did not take anything, and even if I had taken, I would only have taken what was mine, feel like this, then people who take bribes, all the more so!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל draws the lesson from what he felt. This closes the series of stories about שוחד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reasoning is a קל וחומר. He did not take the fruit, and the fruit was his own anyway, yet he still felt biased. So someone who really takes a bribe from another person's money will surely be biased.

keyTerms.meaning: May their souls be blown away, a curse
How much more so, the language of a קל וחומר

steps.whatToRemember: Any favor, even a tiny one or a gift of your own property, can bias a judge. That is why great judges stepped aside from cases where they had received even a small kindness.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the halacha of שוחד is so strict. A judge cannot trust himself to stay fair once he has received any benefit.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: תִּיפַּח נַפְשָׁם שֶׁל מְקַבְּלֵי שׁוֹחַד!
phrases.english: He said: May the souls of those who take bribes be blown away!
If I, who did not take,
and even if I had taken, I would have taken my own, am like this,

phrases.aramaic: מְקַבְּלֵי שׁוֹחַד — עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: those who take bribes, how much more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the bias רבי ישמעאל felt in step 18.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If a refused gift of one's own property creates bias, then real bribes surely blind a judge.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל בר אלישע refuses the first shearing
steps.stepSummary: A man brings ראשית הגז to רבי ישמעאל בר אלישע. When he admits he has a case, רבי ישמעאל disqualifies himself and refuses the gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man brought רבי ישמעאל בר אלישע the first shearing. He asked: 'Where are you from?' The man said: 'From such-and-such place.' 'Was there no כהן between there and here to give it to?' The man said: 'I have a case, and I thought I would bring it to the Master on my way.' He said: 'I am disqualified from your case,' and he did not accept it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story. A man went out of his way to give a כהן-gift to רבי ישמעאל because he had a case, so רבי ישמעאל refused it and stepped down as judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ראשית הגז belongs to a כהן anyway, so the man was not really giving away anything extra. Still, picking this particular כהן because of the case made it look like a favor, and that was enough to disqualify the judge.

keyTerms.meaning: The first wool shorn from one's sheep, which is given to a כהן
A priest; the one entitled to receive ראשית הגז
I am disqualified from judging your case

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha:

phrases.aramaic: אַיְיתִי לֵיהּ הַהוּא גַּבְרָא רֵאשִׁית הַגֵּז.
phrases.english: a certain man brought him the first shearing.
phrases.notes: This is the first wool from the sheep, a gift that goes to a כהן. רבי ישמעאל was a כהן.

phrases.english: He said to him: Where are you from?
He said to him: From such-and-such a place.
And from there to here,
was there no כהן to give it to?
He said to him: I have a case,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמֵינָא, אַגַּב אוֹרְחַאי אַיְיתֵי לֵיהּ לְמָר.
phrases.english: and I said: on my way, I will bring it to the Master.
He said to him: I am disqualified from your case,
and he did not accept it from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בַּר אֱלִישָׁע אַיְיתִי לֵיהּ הַהוּא גַּבְרָא רֵאשִׁית הַגֵּז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another story to the series of judges who disqualify themselves over small favors.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a gift the judge is already entitled to disqualifies him if it was given because of the case.

steps.title: He appoints other judges but still finds himself leaning
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל seats two rabbis to judge the case. As he walks back and forth, he keeps thinking up arguments the man could make.
steps.simpleTranslation: He seated a pair of rabbis, and they judged the case. As he walked back and forth, he said to himself: 'If he wants, he can claim this, and if he wants, he can claim that.'
steps.whatsHappening: Just like in the earlier story, the judge steps aside, yet his mind keeps working on the man's side of the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא repeats the same wording it used in the earlier story about רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי. The point is the same here: even a refused gift that was only offered pulled his thinking toward the giver.

keyTerms.meaning: A pair of rabbis, appointed as judges
Going and coming; walking back and forth

phrases.english: He seated a pair of rabbis for him
and they judged his case.
As he was going and coming, he said:
If he wants, he can claim this,
and if he wants, he can claim that.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹתֵיב לֵיהּ זוּגָא דְרַבָּנַן וְקָדָיְינִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story and shows the effect of the offered gift on his thinking.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An offered gift biases the judge's mind, even after he has stepped aside.

steps.title: An even stronger lesson about bribe-takers
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל curses bribe-takers. He argues: if I am biased though I took nothing, and even if I had taken it, it was mine anyway, then bribe-takers are surely biased.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'Blast the souls of those who take bribes! If I, who took nothing, and even if I had taken, I would have taken what is mine, am like this, then those who take bribes, all the more so.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל draws the lesson from his own experience, using a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same קל וחומר, in the same words, that רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי made in step 19. There are two reasons he should not have been affected: he did not take the gift, and even if he had, ראשית הגז was due to him as a כהן. If he was still biased, real bribery surely twists a judge.

keyTerms.meaning: May their souls be blown out (a curse)
I would have taken what is mine
All the more so (the closing words of a קל וחומר)

steps.whatToRemember: Even a gift that the judge is fully entitled to bends his judgment, so a real bribe certainly does.

phrases.english: He said: Blast the souls
of those who accept bribes!
If I, who did not take anything,
and if I had taken, I would have taken what is mine, am like this,

phrases.aramaic: מְקַבְּלֵי שׁוֹחַד — עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: then those who accept bribes, all the more so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the moral of the story with the same קל וחומר used in step 19. Here 'mine' means the ראשית הגז he was entitled to as a כהן.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If even a gift owed to the judge biases him, actual bribery surely corrupts judgment.

steps.title: רב ענן refuses a basket of fish
steps.stepSummary: A man brings רב ענן a basket of small fish. When he says he has a case, רב ענן refuses the gift and disqualifies himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man brought רב ענן a basket of small fish. He asked: 'What is your business here?' The man said: 'I have a case.' He did not accept it from him, and said: 'I am disqualified from your case.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another story of a judge refusing a gift from someone with a case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the gift is not something owed to the judge. It is a plain present, so refusing it is the obvious move. The new part of this story comes in the next step, when the man argues back.

phrases.aramaic: רַב עָנָן אַיְיתִי לֵיהּ הַהוּא גַּבְרָא
phrases.english: A certain man brought to Rav Anan
a basket of small fish.
He said to him: What is your business here?
He said to him: I have a case.
He did not accept it from him.
He said to him: I am disqualified from your case.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב עָנָן אַיְיתִי לֵיהּ הַהוּא גַּבְרָא כַּנְתָּא דְגִילְדָּנֵי דְּבֵי גִילֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new story in the same series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge refuses a gift from someone with a case before him and disqualifies himself.

steps.title: The man asks רב ענן to take the gift anyway
steps.stepSummary: The man says he no longer needs רב ענן to judge, but asks him to take the gift so he will not lose the chance to 'bring ביכורים'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'I don't need the Master's judgment. Let the Master accept it anyway, so the Master does not stop me from bringing ביכורים.'
steps.whatsHappening: The man argues back. He drops the case and asks רב ענן to accept the gift for a different reason, a מצוה. This sets up the source he is about to quote.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man changes what the gift is. It is no longer tied to the case. Now it is presented as a מצוה, and he hints that giving to a scholar counts like ביכורים, which the next steps will prove.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master, a respectful way to address a rabbi
First fruits brought to the בית המקדש and given to a כהן

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּינָא דְּמָר לָא בָּעֵינָא,
phrases.english: He said to him: I do not need the Master's judgment;
but let the Master accept it anyway,
so that the Master does not prevent me from bringing first fruits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The man responds to רב ענן's refusal with a new reason to accept the gift.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Giving a gift to a scholar is a מצוה, so refusing it takes that מצוה away from the giver.

steps.title: A פסוק about a gift brought to אלישע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא citing the פסוק about a man who brought 'bread of ביכורים' to אלישע.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'And a man came from בעל שלשה, and brought the man of God bread of first fruits, twenty loaves of barley and fresh grain in his sack.'
steps.whatsHappening: The source for the man's claim begins with a פסוק. This sets up a question about it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse calls a gift to אלישע, the 'man of God', ביכורים. That wording is the starting point for the lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: Man of God, meaning the prophet אלישע

phrases.english: As it is taught: "And a man came from Baal Shalisha,
and he brought the man of God bread of first fruits,
twenty loaves of barley,
and fresh grain in his sack."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source behind the man's claim.
steps.raayaObject: That a gift to a תלמיד חכם counts like ביכורים
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים ב 4:42, quoted in a ברייתא

steps.title: אלישע could not eat ביכורים
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks: was אלישע someone who ate ביכורים? So why does the verse call the gift ביכורים?
steps.simpleTranslation: But was אלישע someone who ate first fruits?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא points out a problem with reading the verse literally. This sets up its answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ביכורים go to a כהן, and אלישע was not one. So the gift could not have been real ביכורים, and the word must be teaching something else.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it so? (opens a challenging question)
The prophet אלישע, who was not a כהן

phrases.english: But was Elisha one who eats first fruits?
phrases.notes: Only a כהן may eat ביכורים, and אלישע wasn't one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the literal meaning of the verse just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The verse's description of the gift to אלישע as ביכורים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ביכורים are eaten only by כהנים, so אלישע could not have received actual ביכורים.

steps.title: A gift to a Torah scholar is like first fruits
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that the verse teaches that whoever brings a gift to a תלמיד חכם is considered as if he brought ביכורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it comes to tell you: whoever brings a gift to a תלמיד חכם, it is as if he brought first fruits.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question. This answer is the source the man relied on when he asked רב ענן to accept the fish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse uses the word ביכורים on purpose, even though the gift was not real ביכורים. It teaches that a gift to a Torah scholar has the value of ביכורים. That is why the man felt that being refused would take away his מצוה.
steps.whatToRemember: The man's argument is that a gift to a תלמיד חכם is like bringing ביכורים, learned from the verse calling the gift to אלישע 'bread of ביכורים'.
steps.confusionAlert: The man is not saying the fish are actually ביכורים. 'As if' means the gift counts like ביכורים in value, not that the laws of ביכורים apply.

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to tell you:
whoever brings a gift to a Torah scholar,
it is as if he has brought first fruits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the question about אלישע and completes the man's proof.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the verse: the word ביכורים is read as a comparison, not literally.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse seems to describe actual ביכורים given to אלישע, which makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse teaches that a gift to a תלמיד חכם is considered like bringing ביכורים.

steps.title: רב ענן accepts the gift once he hears the reason
steps.stepSummary: רב ענן says he did not want to accept the gift. Now that the man has explained his reason, the chance to bring ביכורים, he will accept it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I did not want to accept it. Now that you told me the reason, I will accept it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ענן answers the man and agrees to take the fish, because the man explained it is a way to fulfill something like bringing ביכורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, רב ענן refused because a gift from someone with a case looks like a bribe. Now the man is not asking him to judge, and the gift has a good purpose, so the problem is gone. Still, as the next step shows, accepting the gift keeps רב ענן from judging this man.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב ענן answering the man who brought the fish.

phrases.english: I did not want to accept it,
now that you have told me the reason,
I will accept it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: קַבּוֹלֵי לָא בָּעֵינַן דְּאֵיקַבֵּיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the story after the ברייתא about אלישע and shows רב ענן acting on the man's reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gift given to a תלמיד חכם for the sake of the מצוה, and not for judgment, may be accepted.

steps.title: רב ענן sends the man to רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: רב ענן sends the man to רב נחמן with a message: please judge this man, because I, ענן, am disqualified from judging him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent him to רב נחמן and wrote to him: Let the Master judge this man, for I, ענן, am disqualified from judging him.
steps.whatsHappening: Because he took the gift, רב ענן still will not judge the man, so he passes the case to רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking the gift was allowed, but it now makes רב ענן unfit to be this man's judge. His note says he is disqualified but does not say why, and that missing reason sets up the next step.

phrases.english: He sent him before Rav Nachman,
and he sent him a message:
Let the Master judge this man,
for I, Anan, am disqualified from judging him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of accepting the gift: רב ענן is now disqualified and passes the case on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge who accepted a gift from someone must not judge that person's case.

steps.title: רב נחמן concludes the man must be רב ענן's relative
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן reasons that since רב ענן wrote he was disqualified, the man must be his relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Since he sent me this message, I can learn from it that he is his relative.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן tries to work out why רב ענן cannot judge, and guesses it is because they are related.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual reason a judge is disqualified is being related to one of the sides, so that is what רב נחמן assumes. The real reason, which we know from the earlier steps, was the gift, and רב נחמן does not know about it.

keyTerms.meaning: learn from it, conclude from this

steps.confusionAlert: רב נחמן's guess is not the real reason. We know from the earlier steps that רב ענן was disqualified because of the fish he accepted.

phrases.english: He said: From the fact that he sent me this,
learn from it that he is his relative.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר: מִדִּשְׁלַח לִי הָכִי, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב נחמן reacts to רב ענן's note and fills in the reason the note left out.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן infers from the note that the man is רב ענן's relative.

steps.title: An orphans' case is before רב נחמן, and he speaks
steps.stepSummary: At that time a case involving orphans was being heard before רב נחמן, and he began to say something.
steps.simpleTranslation: A case of orphans was standing before him. He said:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא tells us what was going on in רב נחמן's court and is about to give his words in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Orphans' cases are usually heard first, so mentioning one here prepares for a decision about the order of cases. What רב נחמן actually says comes next.

phrases.english: A case involving orphans was standing before him,
He said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the scene in רב נחמן's court after his conclusion, leading into his next statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line introduces what רב נחמן will say.
